rules.statement: In a test project, when a test needs to check how many times a strict mock is called, put the count on the setup with `.Verifiable(Times.Exactly(n))` instead of calling `mock.Verify(..., Times...)` by hand.
rules.why: Call counts then follow the verified-mock pattern: they are verified when the test class disposes its mocks, not checked by hand.
rules.check: Look for `mock.Verify(` calls with a `Times` argument in test methods, where the setup could carry `.Verifiable(Times...)` instead.

rules.statement: In a test project, name each test method for everything it checks, not just part of it, such as only one of the two entities whose behavior it asserts.
rules.why: If the name leaves out something the test checks, a reader can't tell from the name what the test covers.
rules.check: Compare the test method name with its setups and assertions, and flag checked behavior or entities the name doesn't mention.

rules.statement: In production code, when more than one place throws the same error response (for example the same not-found `HttpResultException` and message), build it in one shared helper that every caller uses, instead of repeating the message inline.
rules.why: If one copy is reworded and the others aren't, the same error comes back with different messages.
rules.check: Look for new code that builds an exception or error result whose message text already appears elsewhere in the codebase, instead of calling a shared error factory.
